title: Green Emotion: Incorporating Emotional Perception in Green Marketing to Increase Green Furniture Purchase Intentions
central_proposition: Emotional perceptions (pleasure, arousal, and dominance) mediate the relationship between green and traditional furniture characteristics and consumers' intention to purchase green furniture.

concept_definitions.name: Perceived green value (PGV)
concept_definitions.definition: The consumer's overall assessment of the net benefits of a product or service based on the consumer's environmental desires, sustainability expectations, and green needs.

concept_definitions.name: Green brand image (GBI)
concept_definitions.definition: A distinct collection of consumer impressions associated with a brand connected to sustainability and environmental concerns.

concept_definitions.name: Aesthetic design (AD)
concept_definitions.definition: The visual appeal and attractiveness of eco-friendly furniture.

concept_definitions.name: Environmental awareness (EA)
concept_definitions.definition: Individuals' consciousness of environmental challenges and their readiness to address them.

concept_definitions.name: Eco-innovation (EI)
concept_definitions.definition: Innovations aimed at minimizing environmental impact by lowering ecological footprint, preventing waste, and promoting reuse.

concept_definitions.name: Perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE)
concept_definitions.definition: How much consumers believe their actions, such as environmentally friendly shopping, help to address societal issues like pollution.

concept_definitions.name: Purchase customization (PC)
concept_definitions.definition: The ability for users to tailor a product's material, appearance, and color to their preferences and requirements.

concept_definitions.name: Subjective norms (SN)
concept_definitions.definition: The perceived societal influences affecting an individual's behavior.

concept_definitions.name: Perceived pleasure (PP)
concept_definitions.definition: Emotional variability measuring happiness, joy, or contentment in surroundings.

concept_definitions.name: Perceived arousal (PA)
concept_definitions.definition: Emotional arousal indicating how excited, alert, or active an individual feels.

concept_definitions.name: Perceived dominance (PD)
concept_definitions.definition: Emotional regulation and the sense of autonomy or control in a given setting.

concept_definitions.name: Green furniture purchase intention (PI)
concept_definitions.definition: A deliberate and thoughtful decision describing why a consumer buys a specific product or brand, impacting eco-friendly purchasing habits.

argument_structure: The paper proposes a conceptual model where green and traditional furniture characteristics act as antecedents to emotional perceptions (pleasure, arousal, dominance) based on the PAD model. These emotional perceptions then serve as mediators influencing consumers' green furniture purchase intentions. The model is empirically tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM).
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism posits that specific attributes of green furniture (e.g., perceived green value, green brand image, eco-innovation) and traditional design elements (e.g., aesthetic design, customization) evoke distinct emotional states (pleasure, arousal, dominance) in consumers. These induced emotional states, in turn, directly influence the consumer's intention to purchase green furniture. For instance, perceived green value and aesthetic design enhance pleasure, eco-innovation and environmental awareness increase arousal, and green brand image and customization foster a sense of dominance, all contributing to purchase intent.

findings.mechanism: Awareness of environmental features and extra value triggers positive emotional responses like satisfaction and happiness, enhancing positive affective experience.
findings.quote: Perceived green value (PGV) (β = 0.308, p < 0.001) [...] all positively impact perceived enjoyment, supporting hypotheses H1

findings.mechanism: Positive impressions and trust in eco-friendly brands impact favorable perceptions and emotional attitudes, leading to increased enjoyment. Green branding evokes emotional resonance.
findings.quote: green brand image (GBI) (β = 0.316, p < 0.001) [...] all positively impact perceived enjoyment, supporting hypotheses H2

findings.mechanism: Visual appeal, attractiveness, ergonomics, comfort, high-quality materials, and sensory experiences enhance perceived pleasure.
findings.quote: attractive design (β = 0.272, p < 0.001) all positively impact perceived enjoyment, supporting hypotheses H3

findings.mechanism: Consciousness of environmental challenges and readiness to address them, leading to concern for ecological issues and preference for eco-friendly attributes, increasing arousal.
findings.quote: Environmental awareness (EA) (β = 0.252, p < 0.001) [...] all had a positive effect on perceived arousal, supporting hypotheses H4

findings.mechanism: Adoption of eco-innovations improves favorable opinions, amplifies positive emotions and trust, raising awareness and interest in environmental matters, eliciting surprise and excitement.
findings.quote: eco-innovation (EI) (β = 0.416, p < 0.001) [...] all had a positive effect on perceived arousal, supporting hypotheses H5

findings.mechanism: Belief that one's actions (eco-friendly shopping) help address societal issues boosts enthusiasm for eco-friendly products, increasing arousal.
findings.quote: perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE) (β = 0.231, p < 0.001) all had a positive effect on perceived arousal, supporting hypotheses H6

findings.mechanism: Positive trust in a green brand increases identification, leading to autonomy over choices and a sense of control when supporting a green brand as an environmental commitment.
findings.quote: green brand image (GBI) (β = 0.293, p < 0.001) [...] all have a positive influence on perceived domination, supporting Hypotheses H7

findings.mechanism: Tailoring products to preferences increases options and authority, boosting sense of control during buying, enhancing connection, and streamlining decision-making.
findings.quote: purchase customization (PC) (β = 0.300, p < 0.001) [...] all have a positive influence on perceived domination, supporting Hypotheses H8

findings.mechanism: Perceived societal approval for eco-friendly purchases boosts intention to comply, increasing sense of dominance.
findings.quote: subjective norms (SN) (β = 0.298, p < 0.001) all have a positive influence on perceived domination, supporting Hypotheses H9

findings.mechanism: Pleasure impacts the consumer's likelihood to purchase and influences approach behaviors.
findings.quote: Hypothesis H10 is supported by the positive effects of perceived pleasure (β = 0.236, p < 0.001) [...] on purchase intention for green furniture.

findings.mechanism: Arousal leads to a positive tendency to interact with the retail setting and raises the possibility of repeating the activity or visiting the same place, influencing approach behaviors.
findings.quote: Hypothesis H10 is supported by the positive effects of [...] arousal (β = 0.369, p < 0.001) [...] on purchase intention for green furniture.

findings.mechanism: The feeling of control resulting from perceived dominance influences behaviors like purchase intention.
findings.quote: Hypothesis H10 is supported by the positive effects of [...] dominance (β = 0.303, p < 0.001) on purchase intention for green furniture.

findings.mechanism: Green features, such as environmental protection and sustainability, are more capable of eliciting emotional responses from consumers compared to traditional features.
findings.quote: The impact of green features (GF) on emotional perception (EP) is more pronounced (β = 0.511, p < 0.001) compared to the effect of traditional features (TC) on emotional perception (EP) (β = 0.390, p < 0.001).

findings.mechanism: Traditional characteristics, while less impactful than green features, still contribute to evoking emotional responses in consumers.
findings.quote: The impact of green features (GF) on emotional perception (EP) is more pronounced (β = 0.511, p < 0.001) compared to the effect of traditional features (TC) on emotional perception (EP) (β = 0.390, p < 0.001).

findings.antecedent: Green features (GF) mediated by Emotional perception (EP)
findings.mechanism: Green qualities of green furniture are more likely to evoke emotional responses from customers, subsequently influencing their intention to purchase green furniture.
findings.quote: the mediating effect of GF→EP→PI (β = 0.460, p < 0.001) is stronger than the mediating effect of TC→EP→PI (β = 0.326, p < 0.001).

findings.antecedent: Traditional characteristics (TC) mediated by Emotional perception (EP)
findings.mechanism: Emotional responses to traditional characteristics, while less impactful than green features, still contribute to influencing purchase intention.
findings.quote: the mediating effect of GF→EP→PI (β = 0.460, p < 0.001) is stronger than the mediating effect of TC→EP→PI (β = 0.326, p < 0.001).

findings.antecedent: Green brand image (GBI) for consumers born after the 1970s
findings.mechanism: Individuals born after the 1970s may have a greater inclination to place trust in established brands and regard environmentally friendly furniture brands with greater importance, leading to increased pleasure.
findings.quote: a green brand image (GBI) significantly influences consumers born after the 1970s, compared to those born after the 1990s, who prioritize pleasure.

findings.antecedent: Perceived green value (PGV) for consumers born after the 1990s
findings.mechanism: Individuals born after the 1990s may exhibit a greater emphasis on sustainable principles and are more inclined to utilize social media platforms, increasing their susceptibility to influence and fostering greater interest and satisfaction with green furniture.
findings.quote: the perceived green value (PGV) has a more substantial impact on consumers born after the 1990s, who experience higher levels of pleasure

findings.mechanism: Women are typically more emotional and focused on emotional experiences, and green furniture may inspire emotional resonance in women through features such as its sustainable philosophy and the aesthetics and style of home décor, making them more likely to desire to buy.
findings.quote: females are more likely than males to be influenced by the features of green furniture, which elicit emotional perception and generate purchase intention.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Perceived green value (PGV) and perceived pleasure (PP) are positively correlated (H1).
A green brand image (GBI) and perceived pleasure (PP) are positively correlated (H2).
Aesthetic design (AD) and perceived pleasure (PP) are positively correlated (H3).
Environmental awareness (EA) and perceptual arousal (PA) are positively correlated (H4).
Eco-innovation (EI) and perceived arousal (PA) are positively correlated (H5).
Perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE) and perceived arousal (PA) are positively correlated (H6).
A green brand image (GBI) and perceived domination (PD) are positively correlated (H7).
Purchase customization (PC) and perceived dominance (PD) are positively correlated (H8).
Subjective norms (SN) and perceived dominance (PD) are positively correlated (H9).
Perceived pleasure (PP), arousal (PA), dominance (PD) and green Furniture purchase intention (PI) are positively correlated (H10).
bridge_warrants: The PAD (pleasure, arousal, and dominance) emotional model is used to analyze how emotional perception affects potential users' intentions to buy green furniture.

The Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) is implicitly referenced through the inclusion of subjective norms and perceived consumer effectiveness as antecedents to emotional states and purchase intention.
methodological_critiques: The data acquired for this study were limited to a cross-sectional perspective, suggesting future analyses should investigate using a longitudinal experimental design.

The study only investigated the impact of green furniture features on consumers' emotional responses, and future mechanisms could explore the dual-mediated impacts of the functional and emotional dimensions.
model_structure: The proposed model integrates green features (Environmental Awareness, Eco-Innovation, Perceived Green Value, Green Brand Image) and traditional characteristics (Aesthetic Design, Purchase Customization, Perceived Consumer Effectiveness, Subjective Norms) as antecedents. These antecedents influence three dimensions of emotional perception (Perceived Pleasure, Perceived Arousal, Perceived Dominance) from the PAD model, which in turn directly influence Green Furniture Purchase Intention. The model also includes mediating effects of emotional perception between characteristics and purchase intention.
limitations: The study used a questionnaire approach, limiting data to a cross-sectional perspective.
The analysis was limited to the emotional influence of intentions to make environmentally friendly purchases in various locations.
The paper only investigated the impact of green furniture features on consumers' emotional responses, and future research could explore dual-mediated impacts of functional and emotional dimensions.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Green Emotion: Incorporating Emotional Perception in Green Marketing to Increase Green Furniture Purchase Intentions
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The industrialization process has led to environmental deterioration, which has created challenges for sustainable development. However, there is an increasing inclination to purchase green furniture as a sustainable form of furniture. Hence, investigating the determinants of consumers’ intention to purchase green furniture is beneficial for promoting the adoption of sustainable furniture. Previous research has examined the functional aspects of purchasing behavior using the theory of planned behavior (TPB), while giving less consideration to affective elements. This study aimed to investigate the factors that influence the intention of future users to purchase green furniture, explicitly focusing on emotional perception. This study utilized the PAD three-dimensional emotion model. A novel conceptual model was developed, drawing upon the findings of the literature review. This study employed the questionnaire method to collect data, resulting in 412 valid samples. The collected data were then analyzed and processed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 3.0 software. Additionally, the mediating influence of the variables was examined using the bootstrap method. The results suggested that the perceived pleasure, arousal, and dominance all had a substantial influence on the beneficial effect of green furniture elements on purchase intention. Among these factors, pleasure (PP) had the strongest mediating effect on the relationship between green brand image (GBI) and purchase intention (PI). Arousal (PA) had the strongest mediating effect on the relationship between eco-innovation (EI) and purchase intention (PI). Dominance (PD) had the strongest mediating effect on the relationship between purchase customization (PC) and purchase intention (PI). Furthermore, this paper examined the disparities between the characteristics of green furniture and conventional furniture in terms of their ability to stimulate emotional responses and influence consumers’ intention to purchase. This study revealed that green features (GF) have a greater capacity to evoke emotional responses in consumers, consequently impacting their intention to purchase green furniture. The study’s findings have both theoretical implications and practical relevance. In theory, these findings enhance the theoretical framework of purchase intention for green furniture. In practice, they provide specific ideas and recommendations for green furniture companies to develop emotional marketing strategies.
